result:
There is a quiet art that no one really teaches you, and it might be the most important one of all: the art of noticing.

Not the big, obvious noticing. Not noticing that it's raining or that you missed your stop or that your phone is buzzing. I mean the small, almost invisible noticing. The kind that happens in the corner of your eye when you're not trying.

I was thinking about this yesterday while waiting for coffee. The shop was crowded, loud, everyone on their laptops or on their phones, the espresso machine screaming. And there was a potted plant on the windowsill that had been there for years, I assume, but I had never really seen it before. It was a pothos, the kind that trails and survives despite neglect. One of its vines had grown so long it had started to wrap itself around the handle of the window, as if it was trying to leave. No one had trimmed it. No one had guided it. It just found the nearest thing to hold onto and held on.

I stared at it for a long time. It felt strangely moving. This little green thing, doing its patient work in a room full of people who were all trying to do their own patient work, mostly alone.

We don't talk enough about how much of the world is just quietly happening without us.

### The Museum of Unfinished Things

If you pay attention, you start to realize that the world is full of unfinished things, and they are beautiful precisely because they are unfinished.

There is a house on my street that has been under construction for three years. The scaffolding went up, then some of the siding came off, then a blue tarp went over part of the roof. Then nothing. For months, nothing. People in the neighborhood gossip about it - money troubles, permit issues, a divorce. No one really knows. But in the meantime, that house has become something else. Sparrows have built a nest in the gap where the gutter used to be. The plywood over the front door has weathered to a soft silver-gray and someone - a kid, maybe - has drawn a small smiley face on it in black marker. Morning glories have climbed the scaffolding.

It was supposed to be a renovation. Now it's a habitat, a canvas, a clock that tells time by rust and vines.

We have this idea that things should be finished, polished, complete. That a life, a project, a person should reach a state of "done." But most interesting things remain gloriously, stubbornly unfinished. The novel in your drawer with three good chapters. The language you learned enough of to order food and ask for directions but not enough to dream in. The friendship that drifted but never officially ended, so that if you ran into each other on a train ten years later, you could just pick it up again.

I have come to love unfinished things more than finished ones. Finished things are closed. They have an answer. Unfinished things still have possibility in them. They are still breathing.

A few years ago I started keeping what I call a "museum of unfinished things" in a notebook. Not a to-do list. Not a list of failures. Just a catalog of lovely loose ends. A sketch of a building I never finished drawing because the pen ran out and I liked it better incomplete. A photo of a half-knitted scarf where I dropped a stitch and decided the hole looked intentional, like a window. A recipe I invented that was almost good but needed something I couldn't name. 

Collecting these things taught me to be gentler with myself. Not everything has to be concluded to be valuable.

### How Memory Actually Works

We think memory is like a video camera, that it records faithfully and plays back. But it isn't. Memory is more like a painter who only had a few seconds to look at the scene.

Neuroscientists will tell you that every time you remember something, you are not retrieving it; you are reconstructing it. You are rebuilding the scene with the materials you have now - your current mood, what you've learned since, what you wish had happened. Each recall is a new painting.

That's why your childhood home seems to get smaller every time you visit it, but larger in your dreams. That's why you and your sibling can have completely different memories of the same Christmas morning and both be right.

I used to find this terrifying - the idea that my past is not stable, that I am an unreliable narrator of my own life. Now I find it comforting. It means the past is not a stone monument. It's clay. We can reshape it a little as we go, not to lie to ourselves, but to understand it better.

When I was twelve, I was convinced I had humiliated myself in front of my entire class during a presentation. I remembered silence, staring faces, a laugh. For twenty years that memory sat like a cold coin in my pocket. Last year I ran into a former classmate who remembered that same day. "Oh yeah," she said, "you were so nervous but you did great, remember Mr. Henderson gave you an A?" The laugh I remembered? Someone dropping their books in the back.

My memory had edited the scene to match how I felt, not what happened.

So much of what we carry is not what happened but the story we told ourselves about what happened while we were trying to make sense of it. And stories can be retold.

### The Attention Economy and the Return of Wonder

We live in a time that is very good at capturing attention and very bad at keeping it. Every app, every headline, every notification is designed by some of the smartest people on earth to make you look, just for a second longer. The result is that many of us live in a state of continuous partial attention. We are everywhere and nowhere.

The cost isn't just time. It's wonder.

Wonder requires sustained, unprofitable attention. It requires looking at something that will not reward you immediately. Staring at clouds until you see faces. Watching ants carry crumbs. Listening to a song all the way to the end even though you already know the chorus.

Wonder is inefficient, and that is its power.

I have been trying to reclaim it in small, deliberate ways. I leave my phone in another room when I go for a walk. At first my brain protested. It kept reaching, phantom-limb style, for the quick hit of novelty. After about fifteen minutes, something shifted. The walk got slower. I started to notice things again: how the bark on one side of a tree is always rougher because of the wind, how the air smells different two streets over near the bakery, how many different kinds of green there are in a single park.

The world comes back when you stop trying to scroll past it.

There is a wonderful term from the Japanese, *komorebi*, which means the sunlight filtering through leaves. There is no direct English equivalent because we didn't think we needed a word for it. But once you learn the word, you see it everywhere, and you realize you needed it all along. Attention creates vocabulary, and vocabulary creates world.

I think we need more words like that. We need words for the way dust hangs in a sunbeam at 4 p.m. We need words for the specific melancholy of a grocery store late at night when the Muzak is playing and the fluorescent lights are too bright. We need words for the feeling that someone is about to text you right before they do.

### An Invitation

If you made it this far, here is my small, unambitious invitation to you: Go find one thing today that is not trying to get your attention, and give it your attention anyway.

It could be the way your coffee cools and leaves a ring on the table. It could be the sound your building makes when the heat clicks on. It could be the hands of someone you love, and how they have changed since you last really looked.

Don't photograph it. Don't post it. Just notice it. Let it be unfinished, imperfect, unshared, and still entirely real.

We spend so much of our lives waiting for big, cinematic moments to feel alive - graduations, arrivals, revelations. But life is not made of those. Life is made of a thousand small, quiet noticings stitched together like light through leaves.

The plant is still in the coffee shop window, still holding onto the handle. I check on it every time I go now. Last week I saw that someone had finally trimmed it, but not too much. Just enough to let it keep growing, but in a slightly different direction. I like to think it doesn't mind.
